title: The Problem of Evil
subtitle: Why this question breaks faith. The logical problem, the evidential problem, and an honest account of the weight.
triageNote: This page does not divide faithful churches against one another. It marks the place where faith itself is most often lost. It is first-order in a different sense than the rest: not because Christians disagree about it, but because it is the single hardest objection the faith faces. A believer who has never felt its weight has not yet been paying attention. The positions below are not rival Christian camps. They are the major ways the problem has been pressed and the major shapes of Christian response. Hold the goodness and power of God. Hold, with equal honesty, the reality of the suffering that makes people doubt both. A faith that will not look at this squarely is not yet a faith that can carry anyone through it.
question: A child dies slowly of a disease no one chose. A good man is tortured by men who go unpunished. An earthquake buries a city that did nothing to deserve it. And the Christian says God is good, and God is all-powerful, and God is in control. Hold those three claims next to the dying child and the question writes itself, the oldest and hardest in the world. If God is good, he would want to stop it. If God is all-powerful, he could stop it. It is not stopped. So either he is not as good as you say, or not as powerful as you say, or not there at all. Epicurus is supposed to have framed it that way more than two thousand years ago. Nothing has dulled it since. This is not a puzzle for seminar rooms. It is the question that empties pews, the one whispered in hospital corridors, the one that has taken more people out of the faith than every clever atheist argument combined. And there are really two versions of it. One tries to prove the Christian God impossible. The other simply asks whether, given all this suffering, belief in him is reasonable. The first can be answered. The second cannot be dismissed. This page takes both seriously. It refuses the cheap comfort that has done so much harm.
whyItMatters:
Most people do not lose their faith over an argument. They lose it over a grave. The problem of evil is where doctrine meets the worst thing that ever happened to you. If the faith has nothing honest to say there, it will not survive there. And it should not pretend to. A Christianity that meets a grieving mother with God's got this, or everything happens for a reason offered too soon, or a tidy explanation of what her child's death was for, is not strong faith. It is faith that has never been to the place she is standing. This question matters more than almost any other because it is the one your people are actually asking, usually silently, often while still in the pew. And the church's habit of answering it too fast and too brightly has driven more honest souls away than it has kept.

It matters, too, because the temptation under pressure is to save God by shrinking him. We are tempted to say he could not help it, or did not really mean it, or that the evil was secretly good if you squint. Every one of those rescues costs something the faith cannot afford to lose. A God who could not prevent your suffering is not the God who promises to redeem it. A God for whom the evil was secretly fine is a God who has not taken your wound seriously. The hardest and most faithful path is to refuse those exits. Keep saying God is good and God is sovereign and this is genuinely evil. All three. Feel the full pressure of holding them together rather than dropping one to ease the ache.

And it matters because the Christian answer, such as it is, does not finally come as an argument at all. It comes as a cross. Whatever else the faith says about suffering, it says that God did not stay above it. He entered it, was tortured by it, cried out under it, died in it. That does not explain your suffering. It does something the explanation could not do. It tells you the God you are angry at is not safe and distant from the thing that is destroying you. He has been inside it himself. Whether that is enough is something each sufferer has to find in the dark. But it is the ground the next page stands on. It is why this question, for all its weight, has not emptied the church entirely.

positions.name: The logical problem of evil
positions.inOneLine: The existence of any evil at all is logically incompatible with an all-good, all-powerful God. The very concepts cannot both be true. The Christian God is not merely unlikely but impossible.
positions.bestCase:
Let me put the sharpest version of the case, the one that claims not just that God is unlikely but that he is ruled out. The argument is a proof, or means to be. Consider the claims a Christian makes. God is omnipotent, able to do anything that can be done. God is omniscient, aware of all suffering. God is wholly good. And a wholly good being, by definition, eliminates evil as far as it can. Put those together. A being who could prevent all evil, who knew of all evil, and who wanted to prevent all evil, would prevent all evil. Yet evil exists, manifestly, in staggering quantity. Therefore no being who is all of those things at once exists. The conclusion is not that faith is hard. It is that the central claim is incoherent, like a married bachelor or a square circle. You are not asking me to believe something improbable. You are asking me to believe a contradiction.

And do not soften the premises too quickly. The standard reply is that God permits evil for the sake of some greater good, or to preserve free will. But examine that. For free will to save the argument, every evil in the world must be tied to some creature's free choice. Yet the child's leukemia chose nothing. The earthquake willed nothing. And even where free will is involved, an omnipotent God, by definition, could have made free creatures who always freely chose the good, since there is nothing contradictory in a person freely doing right every time, people do it all the time on small scales. If God could have made a world of free creatures who never sinned and did not, then free will does not get him off the hook. The greater-good defense fares no better against the sheer scale and pointlessness of so much suffering. Tie God's hands with logic and the conclusion follows: the God of the philosophers and the Sunday school cannot exist as advertised. That is the hardest form of the objection, and I state it at full strength so that no one pretends it is weaker than it is.

positions.name: The evidential problem of evil
positions.inOneLine: Even granting that evil and God are not strictly contradictory, the kinds and quantities of suffering we actually see make the existence of a good and all-powerful God improbable. The apparently pointless suffering most of all. That is a weight of evidence faith must bear.
positions.bestCase:
I will concede something the logical version will not, and the concession makes my case harder to answer, not easier. I grant that there is no strict contradiction between God and the mere existence of some evil. Perhaps a good God could have morally sufficient reasons to permit suffering. I am not claiming a proof. I am claiming something more modest and, I think, more devastating: that the actual evil we observe, in its kind and quantity and apparent pointlessness, counts as strong evidence against a good and all-powerful God, the way a body with a knife in its back counts as evidence against the story that the man died of natural causes. You do not need a proof to find a belief unreasonable. You need the weight of the evidence to tell against it.

Consider what we actually see. Not just the suffering that might build character or flow from free choice, but the suffering that seems to do nothing at all. A fawn burning to death slowly in a forest fire no human will ever know about, William Rowe's famous example, suffering with no observer, no lesson, no soul to be made. A child abused in secret and then dead, the cruelty never redeemed, never used, never even witnessed. Millions of years of animals tearing each other apart before a single person existed to learn anything from it. The defender of God says all of this serves some greater good we cannot see. But notice what that costs him: he must claim that every instance of apparently pointless suffering, every one, secretly has a point, and he cannot show it for a single case. At some point the repeated appeal to hidden reasons stops being an explanation and becomes a refusal to look at the evidence. I am not saying God is impossible. I am saying that if you weigh the world honestly, the staggering, distributed, often pointless-looking suffering of it tilts the scales, and the believer is believing against the evidence, not with it. That is a quieter argument than the logical one, and a far harder one to shake off, because it does not ask you to find a contradiction. It asks you to look at the world and say honestly whether it looks like the work of perfect goodness and perfect power.
advocates: much of contemporary philosophy of religion
the ordinary unbeliever at the graveside

positions.name: The honest Christian reckoning
positions.inOneLine: The logical problem can be answered. The evidential problem must be carried rather than solved. The faith does not finally meet evil with an explanation but with a God who entered it, so the right response holds firm trust and unresolved weight together.
positions.bestCase:
Let me say first what I will not do, because the failures here have been as damaging as the objection. I will not tell you the suffering was secretly good. I will not tell you it all happened for a reason I can name. I will not hand you a system that ties the dying child into a neat plan and asks you to feel better. Every one of those answers has driven people from God, and rightly, because they are not true to the weight of the thing, and they make God smaller and crueler than he is. The honest Christian reckoning begins by conceding to the objector everything that is real in the objection. The suffering is genuinely evil. It is not a trick of perspective. God hates it more than you do.

Now, a careful distinction, because it matters. The logical problem, the claim that God and evil are flatly contradictory, can be answered, and I think has been. It is not contradictory for a good and powerful God to permit an evil he could prevent, provided he has a sufficient reason, and no one has ever shown that he could not have one. So the charge of strict impossibility fails. But I will not pretend that disposing of the logical problem disposes of the real one. The evidential problem remains, and I do not think it is solved so much as carried. The honest believer does not have an answer to the fawn in the fire or the child abused in secret. What the believer has is a set of reasons to keep trusting God anyway, in the teeth of evidence he cannot fully account for: the reality of his own encounter with God, the testimony of others, the resurrection as a down payment on a world made right, and above all the cross.

Because here is what the faith finally offers, and it is not an argument. When the question is asked at its sharpest, where is God in this, the Christian answer is not a theodicy. It is a location. He is on the cross. The God you are tempted to accuse of watching your suffering from a safe distance is the God who came down into it, was tortured by the very evil you are protesting, and cried your own cry, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, with no answer given in the moment. Christianity does not explain your suffering. It refuses the safe and distant God and gives you instead a God with wounds. And it makes a promise it stakes everything on, that the suffering is not the last word, that the one who entered death came out the other side, and that the world will be set right, every tear wiped away, in a future where the present horror will not be explained away but redeemed. Whether that is enough you will only find out in the dark. But it is not nothing, and it is not a lie, and it is the most honest thing the faith has to say: not here is why, but here is where God is, and here is where this ends.
advocates: Dietrich Bonhoeffer (only the suffering God can help)

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The problem stated from inside Scripture
biblicalEvidence.summary: You who are of purer eyes than to see evil and cannot look at wrong, why do you idly look at traitors and remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he? The prophet presses the problem of evil directly to God's face: how can a holy God watch this and do nothing.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any glib defense, since Scripture itself raises the objection in its sharpest form, accusing God of looking on at injustice and staying silent.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The objector reads Habakkuk as proof the problem is real and biblical, not an outsider's invention. The honest Christian reckoning reads it as God's own word legitimizing the protest: that the Bible puts the accusation in a prophet's mouth shows the faith does not forbid the question but invites it, and Habakkuk ends not with an answer but with a decision to trust through the dark.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The one psalm that does not climb back into the light. It ends, the darkness is my closest friend. A prayer of unrelieved anguish, included in Scripture without a tidy resolution.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any theology that insists every faithful response to suffering must end in resolution and praise, since this prayer ends in darkness and is still holy Scripture.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The honest Christian reckoning treasures this psalm as permission: God put a prayer with no happy ending in his own book, which means the believer in unrelieved darkness is not faithless but is praying a prayer Scripture itself prays. The objector notes that Scripture's own honesty about despair confirms the weight is real. Both agree the psalm refuses cheap comfort.

biblicalEvidence.summary: After thirty-seven chapters of Job's protest and his friends' bad explanations, God answers Job out of the whirlwind, not with reasons but with questions: where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? God never tells Job why.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that God owes the sufferer an explanation, since God's answer to the most famous sufferer is not a theodicy but a self-disclosure that reframes the question.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The honest Christian reckoning reads this as decisive: the book that most directly addresses innocent suffering ends with God refusing to explain and instead giving himself, and Job is satisfied not by an answer but by an encounter. The objector reads God's non-answer as a tacit admission there is no answer to give. Both agree the explanations Job's friends offered, the tidy theodicies, are the thing God rebukes.

biblicalEvidence.summary: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? God incarnate, on the cross, cries the very question of the sufferer, the protest of abandonment, and receives no answer in the moment.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any picture of a God safe and distant from suffering, since God himself, in Christ, cries the cry of the forsaken and enters the abandonment.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The honest Christian reckoning reads this as the center of the Christian response: the answer to the problem of evil is not an explanation but the presence of a God who entered it and cried the sufferer's own cry. The objector notes that even God incarnate is given no answer in the moment, which underscores that no answer is forthcoming. Both agree the cross places God inside the suffering rather than above it.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The Christian hope, contested in its weight
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul holds that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed, that the whole creation groans, and that it waits to be set free. The answer is cast forward, into a future redemption, while the present groaning is named, not denied.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a view that the future glory cancels the present horror, since Paul names the groaning of all creation even while pointing beyond it, and hard for the objector, since the suffering is set against a promised redemption, not left as the final word.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The honest Christian reckoning reads this as the shape of the Christian answer: not present explanation but future redemption, held in hope while the groaning is fully admitted. The objector presses that a future payoff does not justify present pointless suffering, and that comparing present agony unfavorably to future glory can sound like minimizing the agony. Both agree Paul refuses to deny the groaning.

biblicalEvidence.summary: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning nor crying nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away. The faith's final word on suffering is its abolition, not its explanation.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the view that Christianity claims to explain suffering, since its ultimate answer is to end suffering and wipe away tears, which presumes there were real tears worth wiping, not illusions.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The honest Christian reckoning reads this as the ground of carrying the unanswered weight: the believer trusts not in a present explanation but in a promised future where the suffering is undone and the tears are real enough to need wiping. The objector asks whether a future consolation can morally outweigh present atrocity, the question of whether even heaven can justify the road to it. Both agree the verse treats the suffering as real, not apparent.

weighing:
My judgment, given as carefully as I know how, because this is the one question where getting the tone wrong does real harm.

I think the logical problem of evil fails, and I say so without triumph, because winning that argument changes almost nothing for the person who is actually suffering. It is not contradictory for a good and all-powerful God to permit an evil he could prevent, so long as he has a sufficient reason, and the atheist cannot show that he could not have one. Alvin Plantinga's work, which the next page takes up, did the careful logical labor here, and most philosophers on both sides now grant that the strict charge of impossibility does not hold. So if someone tells you the existence of God is simply ruled out by suffering, that overreaches, and you may say so.

But I will not let that small victory become a large evasion, and this is where I part company with a lot of confident Christian apologetics. The evidential problem is not refuted by refuting the logical one, and the kinds and quantities of apparently pointless suffering in this world are a genuine weight, not a riddle I can dissolve. I do not have an explanation for the child abused in secret or the animal suffering of the long ages before us. When a defender insists that every such case secretly serves a good we cannot see, I notice that the appeal to hidden reasons can be made about literally anything, and that it comforts no one standing at the grave. So I hold the evidential problem as something carried, not solved. The honest believer lives with an unanswered question, and trusts God in spite of it, on other grounds, rather than pretending the question has gone away.

And here is the heart of where I land. The Christian faith does not finally answer the problem of evil. It does something stranger and, I have come to think, deeper. It refuses the God who watches from a safe distance and gives you instead a God on a cross, tortured by the evil you are protesting, crying the cry of the forsaken, and then a promise that this is not the end. That is not a theodicy. It is a presence and a hope. I cannot prove it is enough. I can only tell you that the people I have watched come through the worst suffering with their faith intact did not come through it because someone explained their pain. They came through because they met, in the dark, a God who had been there before them. Hold the goodness of God and the reality of the evil at the same time, refuse every cheap answer, and stand at the cross. That is the most honest thing I know to say.
charitableDisagreement:
This is the place to be gentlest, because the person pressing this question is often not a debater but a sufferer, and treating their grief as an argument to be won is its own kind of cruelty. If someone has walked away from God over the death of a child, the worst thing you can do is hand them a tidy theodicy, and the second worst is to act as though their objection is intellectually weak. It is not weak. It is the strongest objection the faith faces, and a Christianity that cannot admit that has not earned the right to speak into the dark. Meet the doubter as Job's God met Job, not with explanations but with presence, and meet the doubter as Job's friends did not, by refusing to explain away a pain you have not felt.

And be honest about the limits of your own answers. The free-will defense, the soul-making story, skeptical theism, the cross, these are taken up on the next page, and each of them helps somewhere and fails somewhere. Do not oversell any of them. A believer who admits I do not know why your child died, but I know where God was when she did is far closer to the truth than one who has an answer for everything.

Is this a hill to die on. In a way it is the hill, because it is the hill so many people actually die on, the place where faith most often ends. But it is not a hill Christians fight each other over; it is a weight the whole church carries together. The goodness and power of God are not negotiable, and neither is the reality of the suffering. Hold both, refuse the cheap exits in either direction, and let the cross be your answer where you have no other.

relatedDebates.note: If the problem of evil is the question, the various theodicies are the attempted answers: the free-will defense, soul-making, skeptical theism, and the cross-centered and protest responses. The next page lays each out at its strongest and asks which, if any, can bear the weight, while keeping in view that an answer and a comfort are not the same thing.

The cross-centered response to evil depends on whether God genuinely enters and shares human suffering. If God is wholly impassible, the comfort that he suffers with us needs careful statement; if God suffers, the comfort is direct but raises other questions. The impassibility page maps that nearby debate.

relatedDebates.topic: Providence and the sovereignty of God
relatedDebates.note: How God governs a world containing evil, whether he ordains it, permits it, or works within a genuinely open future, shapes what you can say about any particular tragedy. The foreknowledge page takes up how God's sovereignty relates to a world where things go terribly wrong.
